Header:
Date: 2026-10-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood CSM); Lena Cho, Marcus Reid, Nina Gupta, Owen Park (HighTide Systems)
Links referenced: Deck - 'Duty Cycle QBR v3' (drive/high-tide/qbr-v3), Cost spreadsheet (drive/high-tide/costs-2026-10), SOC2 excerpt (shared link)

Summary (auto): quick QBR focused on duty-cycle patterns, cost levers (batching, quantization), reliability during peak windows, and roadmap alignment for private deployment pilot. Agreed to run targeted benchmarks and deliver cost scenarios.

[00:00] Alex Morgan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we wanted to focus today's QBR on the duty cycle you described in the pre-read, and nail down the pilot runway. Quick intros?
[00:12] Lena Cho: thanks Alex, lena here - head of ML at HighTide. I'll be the primary for modeling and success criteria.
[00:18] Marcus Reid: Marcus, VP Eng, watching the infra bits and ops constraints.
[00:22] Nina Gupta: Nina, FinOps, i'll own cost sign-off and budgets.
[00:26] Owen Park: Owen, SRE, i'll help with peering and network.
[00:30] Priya Patel: Priya from Redwood, SE, i'll pair with Alex on cost/latency tradeoffs and run the bench work.

[02:05] Alex Morgan: Recap of what you told us — you have a low steady state (around 100 rps) with three short daily spikes up to ~1.6k rps for ~7-9 minutes when the pricing engine recalculates. you call that the 'duty burst'. Is that right?
[02:25] Lena Cho: yeah that's the duty burst, we call it duty-cycle in our docs, it's short but critical for SLA. latency at peak really matters.

[04:10] Marcus Reid: main constraint is we can't take more than 12ms added latency on the 95th at peak, otherwise the orchestration fails. also we're limited on network egress and prefer VPC peering; egress cost is a big line item.
[04:35] Nina Gupta: and from finance the absolute monthly spend needs to stay within the committed band, or we revisit vendor selection next quarter.

[06:00] Priya Patel: ok so tradeoffs: hosted bursts vs dedicated reserved capacity with burst lanes. We showed a three-scenario cost slide in the pre-read: pure hosted, dedicated with 2x burst capacity, and private deployment in your us-east-1 VPC. The biggest lever is batching + KV caching for repeat prefixes during the duty burst which can lower per-token cost and reduce kernel overhead.
[06:35] Lena Cho: can you explain the KV cache bit again, because our prompts have variable prefixes - some repeated, some unique.
[06:51] Priya Patel: sure. KV cache stores the key/value attention cache across tokens so if you have repeated prefixes for a class of requests, the runtime can reuse those cached KV slices - we sometimes call it prefix caching. If your prefixes vary, then effectiveness drops. but even partial reuse helps with latency and cost. our recent customers saw 12-30% token reduction during burst when prefix reuse is medium.

[09:10] Marcus Reid: what's the expected tail latency with heavy batching? we worry batching could push single-request latencies too high during the duty-window.
[09:22] Priya Patel: batching is workload-aware: you can set latency SLOs and the serving runtime does continuous batching within those constraints. for example, with a 20ms tail target, we batch aggressively up to the point it would violate SLO. the other lever is tiny quantized instance types for background traffic and heavier instances only during burst.

[11:00] Alex Morgan: we included a 'burst-lane' proposal - essentially a mix of reserved capacity and short-lived burst instances. the pricing spreadsheet shows blended per-token in the three scenarios. Nina, does the blended metric align with Finance?
[11:18] Nina Gupta: yes that's helpful, but need clearer per-feature line items: embeddings, long-form generation, rerank. Also run rates for peak windows — we need to tie to committed spend bands.

[12:40] Owen Park: on the private side, network peering with VPC is doable but we have MTU differences with your infra and net egress policies. we'll need a short network test.

[14:05] Priya Patel: action item - we'll run a network probe and a 1k-request mini-benchmark (512 token median) to surface egress and latency numbers. That will give concrete numbers for blending hosted/dedicated.

[16:00] Lena Cho: curious about model rollouts and rollback speed. when you do a canary, what's the error surface? our team wants to ensure model quality regressions are caught quickly.
[16:22] Priya Patel: good question - rollouts are per-route, canary at 5-10% with automatic quality checks tied to your eval set. if quality drifts, we auto-fallback to prior model variant. that log and drift alert can feed into your monitoring. notes: occasionally the auto-transcribed docs say 'canary falls' which is wrong, but it's 'fallback'.

[18:40] Marcus Reid: do you keep detailed token-level traces for debugging? we need audit logs for token cost attribution and for compliance.
[18:52] Jordan Lee: yes we provide token-level breakdowns in Console and can export to your SIEM - also we can push structured traces for request IDs.

[20:30] Alex Morgan: security checklist — SSO/SAML, RBAC, KMS integration? Jordan has the SOC2 pack.
[20:38] Jordan Lee: i'll share the SOC2 + SAML integration guide and the KMS notes. for on-prem/private we support customer-managed KMS/HSM and detailed audit logs.

[22:10] Nina Gupta: two security questions: can logs be filtered to remove sensitive PII? and who holds the encryption keys for private?
[22:25] Jordan Lee: logs can be redacted via our redact pipeline or you can forward only metrics. in private, customer-managed KMS means you hold keys; our control plane stores only encrypted artifacts.

[24:00] Priya Patel: circling back to cost optimization: quantization profiles are another lever; for your use-case we recommend int8 for rerank and int4 tests for chat generative if quality loss is acceptable. We'll propose a quantization matrix after the bench run.

[26:15] Lena Cho: quality metrics - we need an objective way to measure quality regression. can you tie to our eval suite?
[26:28] Priya Patel: yes, we can run your eval set during canary and produce a drift score and output diffs. that will be part of the mini-benchmark.

[28:05] Marcus Reid: about SLA: during burst windows the tail 95th is critical. if you fall short, what are remediation paths? hot spare lanes?
[28:18] Alex Morgan: remediation includes automatic fallback to a smaller model to keep latency, pre-warmed burst instances, or route to dedicated lanes. We'll add a postmortem playbook and a runbook for your on-call.

[30:45] Nina Gupta: any hidden costs we should watch for? egress, model variants, and developer test calls?
[30:55] Alex Morgan: yes dev/test calls can leak costs — we recommend dev quotas and token limits. we'll include guardrails in the next proposal.

[32:10] Owen Park: can you show a deployment diagram for the private pilot? we need to understand peering and failover.
[32:22] Priya Patel: (shares screen - link in the deck) the private pilot uses a private control plane with customer VPC peering, optional on-prem agent for air-gapped portions, and a dedicated GPU pool. failover routes to hosted in the same region as a last resort.

[34:50] Lena Cho: timeline question - if we greenlight a limited pilot, how long to stand up the private pilot?
[35:05] Alex Morgan: typical is 4-6 weeks for a scoped pilot: network, small dedicated pool, KMS integration, and pilot rollouts. that assumes we have the network info and a PO for the reserved baseline.

[36:45] Marcus Reid: cost scenarios - can you walk through the blended calculation for a typical month?
[36:55] Alex Morgan: yes - in the sheet we modeled steady-state compute, peak-burst amortized over month, egress, and storage. we blended reserved cost by amortizing reserved instances across the month and counting burst instances as on-demand. the sheet also allows toggling quantization and cache effectiveness.

[39:10] Nina Gupta: as long as the sheet shows line items we can present to procurement. Please include an option that keeps us inside the committed band with a capped burst allowance.

[40:40] Priya Patel: agreed. we'll add a 'capped burst' row and simulate 95th tail under that cap.

[42:00] Alex Morgan: ok recap: Priya runs network probe + 1k bench, Alex sends three cost scenarios + capped burst option, Jordan shares SOC2/SAML/KMS docs, Nina shares forecast & duty-cycle windows, Owen shares peering contacts and MTU details.

[43:15] Lena Cho: that sounds good. also ask: can we have a weekly sync during the pilot?
[43:22] Jordan Lee: yes Jordan will host a 30-minute weekly pilot sync starting when bench starts.

[45:00] Marcus Reid: one last thing — competitor angle. we're evaluating Bedrock for a pure hosted option, but the lack of observability and rollout controls is pushing us to consider Redwood's dedicated mix.
[45:18] Alex Morgan: understood. we'll emphasize observability and rollback controls in the pilot.

[46:00] Nina Gupta: ok thanks everyone - please send items asap so procurement can move.
[46:12] Alex Morgan: thanks all, we'll follow up.

Auto Summary (end): Benchmarks and cost scenarios agreed as next steps; pilot runway and security docs to be shared. Action items and owners captured in the metadata.
